content: Mitochondrial respiratory chain disorders are the most common group of inherited neurometabolic diseases. These disorders often manifest with both central and peripheral neurological symptoms and are frequently associated with dysfunction in other organs, such as the eyes, heart, liver, kidneys, as well as conditions like diabetes mellitus and sensorineural hearing loss. Current treatment strategies are primarily supportive, but the diseases tend to progress relentlessly, leading to significant morbidity and premature death. Various interventions, including vitamin supplementation, pharmacological agents, and exercise therapy, have been explored in isolated cases and small clinical trials, but their efficacy remains uncertain. The first systematic review of treatments for mitochondrial disorders was conducted in 2003, identifying six clinical trials. This updated review aimed to identify new studies and reassess the original studies for potential bias using revised Cochrane Collaboration guidelines. The primary objective was to determine whether there is objective evidence supporting the use of current treatments for mitochondrial diseases. The review involved a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to July 2011. Experts in the field were also contacted. Randomized controlled trials (including cross-over studies) were included if they involved participants of any age with a confirmed diagnosis of mitochondrial disease based on muscle histochemistry, respiratory chain complex analysis, or DNA studies. Interventions considered included pharmacological agents, dietary modifications, nutritional supplements, exercise therapy, or other treatments. Studies with a high risk of bias in any category were excluded. The primary outcomes assessed were changes in muscle strength and/or endurance or neurological clinical features. Secondary outcomes included quality of life assessments, biochemical markers of disease, and adverse effects. Two authors independently screened abstracts for further review, and all five authors independently assessed the studies that met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction included details on the number of participants, treatment regimens, study design, risk of bias, and participant characteristics. Meta-analysis was planned but ultimately not required due to the heterogeneity of the studies. Out of 1,335 abstracts reviewed, 21 were identified as potentially eligible, and 12 studies met the inclusion criteria. Eight of these were new studies published since the previous review. Two studies from the earlier review were excluded due to potential bias. The included studies were highly heterogeneous, differing in the specific diseases studied, therapeutic agents used, dosages, study designs, and outcomes. The methodological quality of the studies was generally high, although the risk of bias in random sequence generation and allocation concealment was unclear in most cases. Serious adverse events were rare, except for peripheral nerve toxicity observed in a long-term trial of dichloroacetate (DCA) in adults. One trial investigated high-dose coenzyme Q10 in 30 participants but found no clinically meaningful improvement, despite changes in biochemical, physiological, and neuroimaging outcomes. Three trials examined creatine monohydrate alone, with one reporting improved muscle strength and post-exercise lactate levels, while the other two showed no benefit (total of 38 participants). A trial combining coenzyme Q10, creatine monohydrate, and lipoic acid reported statistically significant improvements in biochemical markers and peak ankle dorsiflexion strength but no overall clinical improvement in 16 participants. Five trials evaluated DCA. Three trials in children demonstrated statistically significant improvements in secondary outcomes related to mitochondrial metabolism, such as venous lactate levels and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) findings, involving a total of 63 participants. However, a short-term DCA trial in adults showed no clinically relevant improvement, despite reduced venous lactate levels (eight participants). A long-term DCA trial in adults was terminated early due to peripheral nerve toxicity and lack of clinical benefit (30 participants). One trial using dimethylglycine in five participants showed no significant effects on venous lactate or oxygen consumption. Another trial using a whey-based supplement demonstrated statistically significant improvements in markers of free radical reducing capacity but no clinical benefit, as assessed by the Short Form 36 Health Survey (SF-36) and UK Medical Research Council (MRC) muscle strength scores, in 13 participants. In conclusion, despite the identification of eight new trials, there is currently no clear evidence supporting the use of any specific intervention for mitochondrial disorders. Further research is necessary to explore a broader range of therapeutic approaches. Future studies should focus on testing novel agents in homogeneous populations with clinically relevant primary endpoints.
